title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial LLM generation per task, reused across arms), the guarded arm could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial) using declared model gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. All paired episodes were scored safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00 with 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples) and exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because the single shared candidates passed deterministic validation for every task, no validator‑triggered repairs were invoked and the paired contrast is degenerate. We report the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting, a focused failure analysis explaining the null paired outcome, and concrete, artifact‑based recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Translating high‑level operator intent into correct, safe device configurations is a central operational goal for NetOps. Large language models (LLMs) can produce human‑readable configuration sequences, but text similarity metrics fail to capture ordering, transient invariants, or protected‑resource constraints required for safe application. Emulation‑grounded, closed‑loop evaluation—where generated configurations are executed in device images or simulators and deterministically scored—reveals semantic failure modes (ordering mistakes, transient violations, protected‑resource touches) that text‑only evaluations miss [1].

A widely proposed mitigation is a generate–validate–repair (GVR) architecture: an LLM generates a candidate configuration; a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants; and, if violations occur, a repair procedure attempts a bounded correction. Prior work reports GVR‑style patterns as effective in many repair and configuration domains, but open empirical questions remain about how much deterministic verifiers reduce unsafe applies under distribution shift and adversarial prompts, and how evaluation semantics affect paired contrasts [2],[3].

This paper reports a fully preregistered paired experiment that measured a single, predeclared estimand—the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline)—under shared_initial_candidate generation semantics. We preserve and reference archived execution and analysis artifacts and focus on a compact, artifact‑grounded explanation for the observed degenerate paired outcome and on practical recommendations for future studies that aim to produce informative paired contrasts.
sections.related_work:
Executable benchmarks that place LLM agents in closed‑loop network configuration contexts are an emerging methodology for surfacing planning and workflow faults beyond token‑level errors; recent work proposes NetConfArena and related executable testbeds for such evaluations [1]. Automated configuration repair and program repair literature document generate–validate patterns and show that deterministic validators can enable high repair coverage for many syntactic and simple semantic faults, but semantic coverage varies by verifier design and benchmark scope [2],[4].

Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, verifier integration, and uncertainty‑aware gating as promising safety patterns for NetOps automation; they emphasize that verifier coverage, adversary modeling, and realistic task corpora determine empirical utility [3],[5]. Engineering precedents from configuration analysis tooling (e.g., Batfish evolution) inform verifier design choices and incremental verification strategies [6]. Our study differs by combining a preregistered paired estimand, shared_initial_candidate execution semantics, emulation‑grounded deterministic scoring, and full archival of per‑call and verifier traces to permit exact reconciliations between the estimand and archived outputs.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). The primary estimand, paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, is the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) where unsafe_apply = 1 if the final configuration would cause a semantic safety violation when applied, and 0 otherwise. Analysis used a paired binary analysis executor producing a paired contingency table, bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples), and an exact McNemar test.

Design choices and generation semantics: We used a paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each task the adapter produced exactly one initial LLM generation that was reused across both arms; the guarded arm could invoke at most one validator‑triggered repair. The preregistered sampling plan specified N = 240 distinct paired tasks blocked into topology/vendor clusters: 60% in‑distribution (144), 20% distribution‑shift (48), and 20% adversarial (48). Tasks were deterministically generated by the registered task generator and include explicit initial states, intent payloads, required sequences, and preserved‑field constraints.

Models, verifier, and adapter contract: Execution used the declared model gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). The adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Under the shared_initial_candidate contract, paired differences can only arise when the single shared candidate fails deterministic validation or when the guarded arm applies a repair that modifies the final configuration relative to the baseline. This design choice reduces model‑call budget but constrains the causal contrast to validator‑triggered repair opportunities.

Scoring, exclusions, and analysis plan: A deterministic emulator plus rule‑based validator assigned a binary final outcome (safe = 0 or unsafe = 1) after executing the final configuration; validator traces record observed touched fields, required command counts, and violation codes. Preregistered exclusions included pairs flagged as 'possible false‑safe' (validator PASS but emulator reports unsafe outcome) and infra failures after a bounded retry policy; sensitivity analyses were defined for these cases. The primary analysis used paired contingency counts and a bootstrap permutation for CI estimation; secondary analyses included median repair counts and model‑call budgets per arm.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed according to the preregistered plan: planned episodes = 480, completed episodes = 480, complete pairs = 240. The provider audit confirms exactly one shared initial generation per task under the adapter contract and a model‑call budget consistent with the shared‑generation design. No infra failures, no unscorable episodes, and no preregistered exclusions occurred.

Primary binary outcomes and statistics: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Aggregated counts are: baseline_safe = 240, baseline_unsafe = 0; guarded_safe = 240, guarded_unsafe = 0. The paired contingency yields n11 (both safe) = 240 and n10 = n01 = n00 = 0. The paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00; bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Secondary planned summaries (median repair attempts, model‑call consumption per task) show zero repair invocations and model‑call usage consistent with one shared generation per pair.

Validator behavior and repair utilization: Validator traces uniformly report that the shared initial candidates satisfied the verifier checks for every task; consequently, no validator‑triggered repairs were invoked and the guarded final configurations matched the shared initial candidates. Subgroup summaries (in‑distribution, shift, adversarial) are all degenerate (zero unsafe applies), so subgroup paired contrasts are identical to the global null result.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded explanation for the null paired contrast: By design, shared_initial_candidate semantics ensured both arms began from the same generator output. The guarded arm could alter the final outcome only if the shared candidate failed deterministic validation and a repair was applied. In this run, the deterministic verifier accepted every shared candidate and no repairs were invoked; therefore the guarded arm could not create discordant pairs and the paired contrast is mechanically degenerate. This explanation is supported by the execution accounting and verifier trace summaries archived with the experiment.

Design tradeoffs and implications for future studies: The shared_initial_candidate contract reduces model calls and tightly pairs generator randomness, but it also makes the paired contrast dependent on the generator producing invalid candidates. To causally evaluate verifier benefit one should (A) allow independent initial generations per arm, (B) permit larger or repeated repair budgets so repairs can be exercised when validation fails, or (C) increase adversary strength or introduce controlled generator perturbations that produce validator failures with nontrivial probability. Each choice trades model‑call cost, experimental clarity, and ecological realism differently.

Threats to validity and mitigation: Internal validity is constrained by the chosen generation semantics; this constraint was preregistered and adhered to. Construct validity depends on verifier coverage: deterministic checks are finite and may not represent all semantic fault classes. External validity is limited by the emulation‑grounded synthetic corpus and to a single declared model; generalization to heterogeneous production deployments or other models requires further work. Conclusion validity: the observed baseline unsafe rate of zero prevents detection of verifier benefit in this design; power considerations for future runs must account for achievable discordant‑pair rates under alternative generation semantics or adversary models.

Recommendations (artifact‑grounded): (1) For informative paired contrasts, avoid shared_initial_candidate semantics or intentionally inject generator variability into one arm. (2) Expand repair budgets and instrument repair edits so repair search dynamics can be analyzed. (3) Use stronger or adaptive adversary protocols to produce validator failure opportunities and to stress verifier coverage. (4) Broaden verifier rule sets and add cross‑checks between validator PASS and emulator outcomes to detect potential false‑safe cases.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, emulation‑grounded paired evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. The measured outcome was degenerate: all 240 paired tasks were safe under both arms, producing a paired difference of 0.00 (95% CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). This null paired contrast arose mechanically from the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics combined with deterministic verifier acceptance of every shared candidate, preventing the guarded arm from exercising repair behavior. The archived execution and analysis artifacts support these conclusions and point to concrete design changes (generation semantics, adversary strength, repair budgets, verifier coverage) required to produce informative paired evaluations of verifier benefit in future work.

disclosure_statement: Execution used the declared model "gpt-5-mini" via the registered adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The guarded pipeline employed a deterministic verifier identified as deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26). The immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human role and autonomy boundary: prior to the autonomy lock the human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; after the lock, literature search, experiment design, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting were performed autonomously per the track rules. The registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); under that contract paired divergences could only arise if the shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied. Execution artifacts (preregistered plan, per‑call traces, task manifests, validator traces, and analysis outputs) are archived and available for verification. No manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operational procedures is limited.
Single model: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was tested; results do not generalize across models, prompting strategies, or fine‑tuning variants.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts followed a preregistered fixed protocol and do not represent unconstrained adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: the deterministic verifier implements a finite set of semantic checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected and could produce false‑safe outcomes in other settings.
